A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FreqEdit study, and their main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices support reliable comparison. The original instruction-generation appendix and qualitative comparisons remain in v2 under different labels.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations on 70 source images, component ablations, quantitative editing results and a human preference study with 60 completed responses.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds frequency-selection experiments, hyperparameter sensitivity results, latent visualizations and a combined-prompt comparison.

M1.justification: Wavelet injection, adaptive weighting, periodic path compensation and quality guidance retain the same procedures. Reversing the definition of the velocity difference while changing buffer subtraction to addition is algebraically equivalent. Descending timestep indices and renaming k to gamma do not change the method.

E1.justification: The 70-image real/synthetic collection and object, attribute, background, style and action editing coverage remain unchanged. Added diagnostics examine existing editing tasks and alternative processing procedures. The new discussion of out-of-distribution inputs does not report an evaluation on such inputs.

E2.justification: The seven named baselines and their participation in Tables 1–2 remain unchanged. Appendix I/Figure 14 adds a single-pass combined-instruction comparator; Figure 6(d) also compares low-frequency-only and all-frequency injection alternatives.

E3.justification: The main 10-turn evaluation, 28 denoising steps, metrics and user-study protocol are retained. New diagnostic protocols include varying one hyperparameter while fixing the others, selectively retaining latent frequency bands for reconstruction, and comparing combined prompts with sequential editing. These are added controls, not revisions to the main benchmark settings.

E4.justification: v2 substantially expands diagnostic coverage beyond the retained component-removal ablations. Figure 6(d) tests frequency selection; Appendix F adds parameter sensitivity; Appendices G–I examine latent/image frequency correspondence, intermediate path compensation and combined versus sequential prompts. These address previously untested design choices and mechanisms.

E5.justification: Figure 7 retains the same curves and error bars, and the human-study aggregation remains equivalent. No new seed counts, repeated-run information, confidence intervals or significance tests are supplied. The added hyperparameter operating ranges are not statistical uncertainty intervals.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2, Figure 7 and the original comparative image grids retain their results. Added qualitative findings concern frequency-selection failures, parameter sensitivity, latent reconstruction, compensation and combined-prompt identity drift. Appendix F newly reports robustness ranges of 1.5–2.5 for alpha_0 and gamma, and 0.2–0.4 for lambda. Figure 2 omits the previously displayed fifth-turn examples.

T1.justification: The reference-velocity derivation in Appendix A is reindexed consistently but remains mathematically equivalent. The paired sign changes in path compensation and rewritten user-score denominator also preserve the mathematics. Appendix G supplies empirical illustrations rather than a new formal assumption or proof.

C1.justification: The central claims about training-free high-frequency preservation and sustained multi-turn editing remain. The conclusion adds a specific applicability qualification: effectiveness may decrease when a single edit covers a large spatial region. This modestly narrows the stated scope without redefining the contribution.

C2.justification: v2 substantially develops the scientific interpretation through explanations of frequency-selection failures, parameter effects, latent frequency correspondence and combined-prompt complexity. Appendix J extends the earlier source-quality limitation with possible out-of-distribution trajectories and reduced discrimination for large-area edits, and introduces training-based future directions.

D1.justification: Figure 2 newly specifies that each filter is applied once to the source image before editing; this is additional disclosure, not evidence of a changed experiment. The new diagnostics document tested parameter values, fixed defaults and selective-band VAE reconstruction. Existing implementation settings, prompt templates and access information are retained.

R1.justification: The same 62 cited works and the main related-work account remain. Appendix I adds a limited positioning argument, using the already cited VINCIE, MTC and FLUX.1 Kontext works to defend multi-turn editing as an independent research problem rather than a combined-prompt substitute.

P1.justification: Editing is localized: Section 4.4 is rewritten, notation and terminology are standardized, and affiliation and acknowledgment text changes. New appendix sections move the instruction-generation material from G to K. Most existing prose and the main section sequence remain intact.

P2.justification: The visual evidence expands substantially through a frequency-selection panel and new sensitivity grids, frequency reconstructions, a compensation heatmap and a prompting comparison. Figure 2 gains failure boxes and drops its fifth-turn column; Figure 4 is redrawn. Existing tables and qualitative grids are retained, with appendix figures renumbered and layout reflowed.

improvement.justification: v2 better supports previously underexamined design choices through frequency-selection controls and sensitivity analyses, while Appendices G–J clarify mechanisms and acknowledge additional failure conditions. These improve explanatory support and transparency. The gain is limited because the added evidence is largely illustrative, while aggregate benchmark results and statistical reporting remain unchanged.
